query: For a high-entropy alloy coating system on a transition metal matrix, what is the relationship between ambient temperature and tribological performance? Please hypothesize the dominant mechanism linking thermal conditions to wear resistance and propose a boundary where performance degrades.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings on transition metal matrices, tribological performance exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with ambient temperature, characterized by an initial improvement due to the formation of a protective tribo-oxide layer, followed by a sharp degradation once the temperature exceeds a critical threshold where the oxide layer becomes non-protective or the coating undergoes thermal softening.
generation.material_initial_state: A dense, single-phase or multi-phase high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 or CoCrFeMnNi) deposited on a transition metal substrate (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V or 316L Stainless Steel) with a grain size in the sub-micron to micron range.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the coated system to dry sliding tribological tests (pin-on-disk or reciprocating sliding) across a controlled ambient temperature gradient ranging from 25°C to 800°C under constant load and sliding velocity.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric air, constant normal load (e.g., 10 N), constant sliding velocity (e.g., 0.5 m/s), and relative humidity < 40% to isolate thermal effects from humidity-induced corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the tribo-layer composition and morphology, specifically the transition from a hard, protective oxide scale (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3) to a soft, viscous, or delaminating oxide layer, coupled with the onset of thermal softening in the HEA coating subsurface.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures (25°C–500°C), the dominant mechanism is 'tribo-chemical hardening,' where frictional heating promotes the rapid formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer that reduces the coefficient of friction and acts as a barrier against abrasive wear, as observed in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 systems [PMC7515071::chunk::000::abstract::cd6baea278]. As temperature rises beyond the critical threshold, the mechanism shifts to 'thermally activated plasticity and oxide instability.' The oxide layer loses structural integrity (becoming viscous or spalling), and the HEA coating experiences a significant drop in yield strength due to thermal softening, leading to severe adhesive wear and material transfer. While refractory HEAs show high strength up to 1200°C [PMC7475834::chunk::001::introduction::97cd4ea6cb], the specific coating system's wear resistance is limited by the stability of the tribo-oxide film rather than bulk yield strength alone.
generation.predicted_outcome: The specific wear rate will decrease by a factor of 2–5 as temperature rises from 25°C to ~400°C, reaching a minimum. Beyond this point, the wear rate will increase exponentially, with a catastrophic failure mode (severe adhesive wear) occurring once the temperature exceeds the predicted boundary.
generation.baseline: The wear rate of the same HEA coating tested at room temperature (25°C) under identical mechanical conditions, serving as the reference for 'improved' or 'degraded' performance.
generation.boundary: The performance degradation boundary is predicted to occur at a temperature range of 550°C ± 50°C, corresponding to the onset of rapid diffusion-controlled oxidation that forms non-protective, porous oxides and the temperature where the coating's yield strength drops below the critical stress required to maintain a stable tribo-layer.
generation.uncertainty: The exact boundary temperature is uncertain due to the specific elemental composition of the HEA (e.g., the presence of Al significantly enhances oxide stability up to higher temperatures compared to Al-free systems) and the potential for phase decomposition (e.g., BCC to FCC transformation) at elevated temperatures which may either enhance or degrade wear resistance depending on the specific alloy system. The uncertainty is estimated at ±50°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of high-temperature sliding tests on an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA coating on a Ti-6Al-4V substrate. Increment the temperature in 50°C steps from 25°C to 700°C. At each step, measure the coefficient of friction (COF) and specific wear rate. Simultaneously, perform post-test cross-sectional SEM and EDS analysis to characterize the tribo-layer thickness and composition, and use in-situ high-temperature XRD to monitor phase stability during sliding.
measurements: Tribo-layer chemical composition (O, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al ratios)
Subsurface grain size and phase fraction (via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the specific wear rate shows a monotonic decrease or remains constant up to 700°C without a distinct minimum, or if the wear rate increases at temperatures below 400°C. Additionally, if the tribo-layer remains protective (dense, adherent) and the coating retains high hardness above 600°C without phase decomposition, the proposed mechanism of 'oxide softening and plasticity' is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
